source.question: e-6184
source.value:
Remember that in the LU factorization of a matrix $A,$ we write $A=LU$ where the matrix $L$ is a unit lower triangular matrix (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal) and the matrix $U$ is an upper triangular matrix:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14058701/assets/98d64291b8e0d4effe6bb1f3006c3d88d2687697355a83c1b092cdfb54ba4188.png)

With that in mind, let's inspect each product in turn.

- The first product is in $LU$ form because the left matrix is a unit lower triangular matrix, and the right matrix is an upper triangular matrix.
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14058701/assets/10a251d4445a3b190e92fa179badfb5e989b577f3c88812334e921522e7a20e5.png)

- The second product is *not* in $LU$ form. Although the left matrix is a lower triangular matrix, it is not a *unit* lower triangular matrix because it does not have $1$'s on the diagonal.
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14058701/assets/515f139b62a15ee4b38066e6225066b527e277e904ea97473d2a9f50f0f595cb.png)

- The third product is *not* in $LU$ form because the matrix on the right is not an upper triangular matrix, as it has a non-zero entry below the diagonal.
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14058701/assets/e377b0ff63ac6d7b3938187e47a3b5bca0087ddb6eee1d2c086835f394cdf6b9.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

source.value:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -7 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 12 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =U.\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$
